implementation_notes: Ruby's standard library queue is bounded by construction: SizedQueue.new(max) suspends push/<< while the queue is full (the documented back-pressure behaviour), and push(item, non_block: true) raises ThreadError instead of suspending, which is the reject policy in one keyword - the consumer side has the same pair in pop/pop(non_block: true). SizedQueue shares its interface with Queue, so switching the bound on or off is a constructor change and the worker loop stays the same. Hand-written buffers are needed only for drop-oldest or coalescing policies the stdlib does not offer, where a Mutex (or Monitor) plus an Array ring is the idiomatic shape.
code_sketch:
q = SizedQueue.new(10_000)             # the capacity is part of the constructor
begin
  q.push(order, non_block: true)       # full => ThreadError, the caller is never suspended
rescue ThreadError
  dropped += 1                         # decided outcome: shed, and count it
end
workers = 4.times.map { Thread.new { loop { process(q.pop) } } }   # pop blocks while empty
pitfalls: SizedQueue bounds items, not bytes: the retained payload is only as bounded as the objects you put in, and pop() hands ownership to the worker.
ThreadError is the same class Ruby uses for other thread misuse, so a broad rescue swallows real bugs; rescue only around the push and re-raise anything unexpected.
Queues live in one process's memory: worker-process deployments (Puma, Sidekiq) need the broker's queue length or a concurrency limit for back-pressure, not a SizedQueue.
